correctness.rationale: The exact projected-resolvent definition is independently reconstructed from arxiv:1909.13059 equation (2.3). Strict min-max Ritz inclusion follows because a nonzero affine polynomial cannot vanish at two distinct spectral levels. The degree-one interpolation formula gives all coordinates, strict monotonicity and the unique first sign horizon. The limit family has exact rational moments (5/18,7/162,25/126) giving eta_±=(10±sqrt(79))/42; ordinary Lanczos Ritz asymptotics give T_poly~2 log L/L. Standard-library packaged verifier passed 65,143 checks, including direct 2x2 matrix projection, exact rational moments, deterministic stress tests and asymptotic examples. Finite tests are corroboration only; proof includes all quantifiers and boundaries.

originality.rationale: The primary shift-and-invert method (Katrutsa–Botchev–Oseledets 2019, eq. 2.3) and the two-node interpolation identity are known. The closest complete published finding concerns ordinary polynomial Lanczos and yields a different compressed exponent. The present combined result derives the transformed-resolvent first horizon and the explicit positive stiff-limit versus vanishing polynomial-Lanczos horizon. This latter quantitative separation is not stated or implied by the earlier polynomial formula alone: its derivation uses the nonlinear inverse-resolvent Ritz transform and the limit of that transformed 2x2 compression. General matrix-function interpolation theory could potentially imply the combined result; publication priority remains uncertain.
residual_risks: General monotone matrix-function interpolation could subsume the new combined stiff-limit law under an alias; none identified.
The published ordinary two-step Lanczos horizon is highly related and shares the interpolation mechanism; the novelty is restricted to the shifted-resolvent and unbounded stiff-horizon separation.
Qiang Ye (2013) full paper download was inaccessible; only the abstract was inspected.

value.rationale: For shift-and-invert approximation to positive diffusion, pole selection controls solver performance but can affect physical nonnegativity. The theorem gives the exact nonnegative time window for every shift, the dimension-minimal inevitable failure, and a nonroutine asymptotic separation: a fixed shift retains a positive horizon while ordinary polynomial Lanczos loses its horizon at order (log L)/L. This supplies meaningful qualitative and quantitative information for selecting low-budget Krylov schemes; no unsupported claim of global error improvement is made.
